extracted.intended_audience: students and instructors of English composition; general writers seeking concise rules for plain English style
extracted.subtask_description: A concise style-and-usage guide for writers and teachers that lists elementary rules of grammar, punctuation, composition principles, common word-usage pitfalls, and spelling guidance to produce plain, vigorous English prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introductory: concentrate on essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: This book aims to give in brief space the principal requirements of plain English style; it concentrates attention on a few essentials (Chapters II and III) — the rules of usage and principles of composition most commonly violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a small set of wide-application rules rather than many special rules (the book gives three rules for comma use and one for the semicolon because these cover most ordinary sentences); after mastering essentials, learners profit most from individual instruction based on their own work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's.
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive singular of nouns by adding 's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow this rule whatever the final consonant (Charles's friend; Burns's poems; the witch's malice). Exceptions: possessives of ancient proper names in -es and -is, the possessive Jesus', forms like conscience' sake, righteousness' sake. Prefer 'the heel of Achilles' in awkward ancient forms. Pronominal possessives (hers, its, theirs, yours, oneself) have no apostrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.description: In a series of three or more terms with a single conjunction, use a comma after each term except the last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: red, white, and blue; gold, silver, or copper. Usage follows Government Printing Office and Oxford University Press. In business firm names the final comma is omitted (e.g., Brown, Shipley & Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether an interruption is parenthetic; if slight, commas may safely be omitted, but never insert one comma and omit the other. If a parenthetic expression is preceded by a conjunction, place the first comma before the conjunction. Always set off certain items with commas: (1) the year when part of a date and the day of the month when following day of week (February to July, 1916; Monday, November 11, 1918); (2) abbreviations etc. and jr.; (3) non-restrictive relative clauses (The audience, which had at first been indifferent, became more interested). Similar principles apply to phrases or dependent clauses preceding or following the main clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause.
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a comma before a conjunction introducing a co-ordinate clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The early records have disappeared, and the story can no longer be reconstructed. Use a comma before and, but, for, nor, or while (when coordinate). If the second member is introduced by an adverb (accordingly, therefore), use a semicolon, not a comma. Connectives so and yet may be either adverbs or conjunctions—use punctuation according to whether the clause is felt co-ordinate or subordinate. If a dependent clause or introductory phrase that requires a comma precedes the second independent clause, no comma is needed after the conjunction. When the subject is the same and expressed once, use a comma if the connective is but; omit the comma with and when the relation is close or immediate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not join independent clauses by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more clauses, grammatically complete and not joined by a conjunction, are to form a single compound sentence, the proper mark of punctuation is a semicolon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolon between independent clauses (Stevenson's romances are entertaining; they are full of exciting adventures). Writing as two sentences or joining with a conjunction + comma are alternatives; semicolon is often best to indicate close relationship. If the second clause is preceded by an adverb (accordingly, besides, then, therefore), a semicolon is required. Exceptions: very short clauses alike in form may permit a comma (Man proposes, God disposes) and colloquial forms in dialogue may use a comma (I hardly knew him, he was so changed) but are inappropriate in formal writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not break sentences in two.
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use periods for commas — i.e., avoid breaking a sentence into two short sentences when a comma would be correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replace erroneous periods with commas when the second fragment continues the thought (Coming home from Liverpool to New York. → coming home ...). Emphatic single-word sentences may be permissible but ensure emphasis is warranted (Again and again he called out. No reply.). Rules 3–6 should be mastered so their application is second nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.description: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence must refer to the grammatical subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dangling participles: Walking slowly down the road, he saw a woman ... (walking refers to he, not the woman). Recast when necessary (He saw a woman ... walking slowly down the road). The same rule applies to participial phrases preceded by conjunctions or prepositions, nouns in apposition, adjectives, and adjective phrases when they begin the sentence. Sentences that violate this rule are often ludicrous or illogical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic.
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the paragraph the unit of composition: one paragraph to each topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subject is slight or treated briefly, one paragraph may suffice; otherwise subdivide into topics and assign one paragraph per topic to aid the reader. Adjust subdivision to length of composition (examples given for book notice, poem report, novel discussion, historical event). Single-sentence paragraphs should generally be avoided except for transition sentences or in dialogue (each speech begins a new paragraph).

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity with the beginning (as a rule).
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, begin each paragraph with a topic sentence; end it in conformity with the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most useful paragraph form: (a) topic sentence at/near beginning; (b) succeeding sentences explain/establish/develop the topic sentence; (c) final sentence emphasizes or states important consequence. Avoid ending with digressions or unimportant details. Transitional sentences may precede the topic sentence or form a separate paragraph. Topic-sentence meaning can be clarified by restatement, definition, negation, illustration, proof, or development; in narration/description the opening may be a concise comprehensive statement or simply indicate the subject. Brief narrative paragraphs often lack a formal topic sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice.
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the active voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active voice is usually more direct, vigorous, and concise (I shall always remember my first visit to Boston. vs. My first visit ... will be remembered by me.). Do not discard passive voice entirely; it is sometimes necessary. Avoid chaining passives (avoid making one passive depend directly upon another). Avoid making a noun that expresses the entire action the subject of a passive where the verb then has no function. Habitual active voice yields forcible writing; many tame sentences can be revived by substituting an active verb for periphrastic expressions (there is / could be heard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Put statements in positive form.
rubrics_metrics.description: Make definite assertions; avoid tame, colorless, hesitating, non-committal language; use not for denial or antithesis, not evasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer positive forms to negatives because the reader wants to be told what is, not merely what is not (not honest → dishonest; did not remember → forgot). Negative words other than not are often strong (The sun never sets upon the British flag). Use antithesis for rhetorical strength when appropriate (Not charity, but simple justice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use definite, specific, concrete language.
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer the specific to the general, the definite to the vague, the concrete to the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific, concrete terms arouse and hold reader attention; use particular instances and significant details to make prose vivid. Even in exposition/argument, give particular instances of application of general principles. Quoted authorities (Spencer, Browning, Ruskin) illustrate the power of concreteness. Avoid abstract vagueness where a concrete image will do.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words.
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigorous writing is concise; a sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid wordy phrases (the fact that → revise out; owing to the fact that; in spite of the fact that; there is/are often superfluous). Replace circumlocutions with direct words (whether → the question whether; no doubt → doubtless; hastily → in haste). Positive statements and active voice often achieve concision. See Chapter V for many specific examples (case, character, nature, system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid a succession of loose sentences.
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a succession of loose sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A series of loose sentences (sentences with the main idea at the beginning and trailing details) can make prose monotonous; vary sentence structure and avoid too many loosely constructed sentences (see Rule 14 in book for examples and corrections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form.
rubrics_metrics.description: Express co-ordinate ideas in similar form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use parallel construction for coordinate ideas (parallelism) so related ideas are expressed in similar grammatical forms; this strengthens clarity and rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related words together.
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep related words together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place words that belong together adjacent so their relationship is clear; misplaced modifiers and separated related words cause ambiguity or absurdity (see examples in book).

rubrics_metrics.name: In summaries, keep to one tense.
rubrics_metrics.description: In summaries, keep to one tense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing, maintain a single tense throughout to preserve clarity and prevent confusion (illustrated by examples in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end.
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the emphatic words of a sentence at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Position emphatic or important words toward the end of the sentence where emphasis naturally falls; use sentence order to highlight important elements (see Rule 18 for examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: A Few Matters of Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Chapter IV: A Few Matters of Form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers conventional matters of form (typographical and formal conventions such as headings, titles, numerals, abbreviations, etc.). (Chapter title is listed; consult chapter for specifics.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Words and Expressions Commonly Misused
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalog of words and expressions commonly misused with preferred alternatives, explanations, and examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives numerous short entries explaining misuse and preferred wording. Sample entries and guidance from the text include: 'People' is a political term distinct from 'the public'; 'phase' should not be used for aspect or topic; 'possess' not to be used as mere substitute for have or own; 'prove' past participle is proved; 'respective/respectively' often omitable; 'shall/will' usage for future/first person; avoid 'so' as a weak intensifier; split infinitives are in disfavor; avoid 'state' as mere substitute for say/remark; avoid 'student body' for students; use 'system' only when necessary; avoid 'Thanking you in advance' (use 'Will you please' or 'I shall be obliged'); use 'he' with distributive antecedents (each, everybody) unless feminine antecedent is required; use 'very' sparingly; use 'point of view' correctly; avoid indiscriminate use of 'while' for and/but/although; 'whom' often misused for who; 'worth while' misused before a noun; 'would' vs 'should' distinctions. Many specific short entries follow this pattern—identify misuse, explain why, give better alternatives, and provide example corrections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance on conventional spellings and commonly misspelled words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that English spelling is by general agreement and sometimes variable; discourages unaccepted simplifications. Provides a list of often-misspelled words (accidentally, criticize, advice, deceive, definite, believe, describe, embarrass, existence, fascinate, separate, principle, privilege, rhythm, etc.). Advises doubling single consonants preceded by a stressed short vowel before -ed and -ing (planned, letting, beginning), with noted exceptions (coming). Recommends hyphenation for to-day, to-night, to-morrow (but not when joined), and writing any one / every one / some one / some time as two words, except 'sometime' when meaning formerly.
